strengths: The proposed method is designed to encapsulate the monophilic property of the graph benchmarks by neighborhood transformer, which shows good improvements compared to the GNN-based approaches.

The efficiency and memory footprint of the proposed model are further optimized by leveraging linear transformer (i.e., Performer) and designing neighborhood partitioning algorithms based on neighborhood size and area.
The introduction of Neighbourhood Transformers (NT) based on the monophily assumption can be viewed as a contribution to graph learning, and its capacity for expansion appears to be advantageous.
The paper is generally structured clearly and well-written.
Experimental results show that the proposed model has comparable or improved performance.
This paper's presentation is good and clear. I can easily follow most of the content.
The experimental section should be comprehensive and cover 10 datasets, including both homophilic and heterophilic graphs.
From Table 1 and Table 2, the performance improvement against the SOTA is decent and appreciated.
weaknesses: The neighborhood transformer is not quite scalable to handle large-scale graphs given the fact that it requires to apply transformers to the neighborhood of all nodes. Despite the partitioning algorithms, the computations are still intense. The partitioning algorithm, while reducing memory, still necessitates processing all neighborhoods, which limits scalability to very large graphs. The computational cost of applying transformers to each neighborhood, even with partitioning, remains a significant bottleneck, especially when considering the quadratic complexity of standard attention mechanisms within the transformer.
There exist a lot of efficient graph transformers which can handle million-scale graphs, which perform well even on heterophilic graphs, e.g., NAGphormer, VCR-Graphormer etc.

From the scalability perspective, the proposed approach was only tested on the graphs with 40k node at most which is not sufficient to demonstrate the optimization from its partitioning algorithms. The experiments do not adequately demonstrate the scalability of the proposed method. Testing on graphs with only 40k nodes is insufficient to validate the effectiveness of the partitioning algorithm for large-scale graphs.

From the evaluation perspective, the paper does not compare with any graph transformer baselines which have been shown to be the SOTA on quite a few benchmarks. The lack of comparison with state-of-the-art graph transformers is a significant oversight. The paper should include a comparison with models like GraphGPS, which have demonstrated strong performance on both homophilic and heterophilic graphs.
Equations 1~3 should be reversed to correctly show the computation orders step-by-step.

Technically, the novelty and soundness of this work is insufficient. To me, the major contribution is the partitioning algorithm which does not seem to be quite neat. E.g., for the size based partitioning, how is the p determined? For the area based partitioning, what are the pros and cons compared to those classic graph partitioning algorithms (e.g., METIS) and sparsification algorithms? The partitioning algorithm, while a practical contribution, lacks a strong theoretical foundation. The paper does not adequately justify the choice of size-based and area-based partitioning over existing graph partitioning methods like METIS, or sparsification techniques. The lack of a clear rationale for the proposed partitioning method weakens the overall contribution.
It is recommended to discuss related work focusing on monophily.

Some aspects of the experimental analysis lack depth. For instance, it is observed that the performance improvement of NT on homophilic graphs is not as significant as on heterogeneous graphs, yet no in-depth analysis is provided.

The paper claims that the proposed method has good expressiveness. However, I found no (theoretical) analysis regarding the expressiveness. Specifically, the paper lacks a formal analysis demonstrating an improvement in expressiveness compared to existing graph neural networks, such as through the lens of the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test or signal processing-based analysis. The claim of 'good expressiveness' needs to be substantiated with rigorous theoretical results.
Why are 2-hop neighbors useful for node classification on graphs regardless of whether they are homophilic or heterophilic?

It looks like the proposed method (from Eq. 1 to 3, Figure 2 c) still utilizes information from 1-hop neighbors. In my understanding, the core idea of this paper is to collect edge messages (from 1-hop neighbors) by Eq. 3 and then let the edge messages interact via a self-attention module Eq. 2. However, overall, no information from 2-hop neighbors is included. Again, this method is simple, but it is highly unclear why it is effective.

Why previous methods cannot capture the information from 2-hop neighbors? If the 2-hop information is that useful, I think many previously proposed methods should be able to capture it. E.g., GPRGNN [1], ACM-GNN [2]. The paper does not adequately explain why existing methods, which can also incorporate multi-hop information, fail to capture the relevant 2-hop information effectively. Methods like GPRGNN can adaptively assign weights to different hops, and it's unclear why the proposed method offers a unique advantage in this regard.
Some baselines are missing [3-5]. After adding them back, the performance advantage of the proposed method is not that significant on datasets Roman Empire, A-ratings, and Tolokers.

The strategies proposed in Section 4.2 are a bit heuristic-based. The partitioning strategy lacks a theoretical justification for its effectiveness. The paper does not provide a formal analysis of why this particular partitioning method is optimal or even near-optimal. The approach seems ad hoc, and the paper would benefit from a more rigorous treatment of this aspect.
The code is not provided, which lowers the reproducibility of this study.
